Article Title: In 2009, Ashton Kutcher co-founded a nonprofit to protect children online; by mid-2026, its technology had flagged nearly 1.4 million suspected abuse files in six months and was used by agencies in 40
Article Text:
Ashton Kutcher's nonprofit detects nearly 1.4 million suspected child abuse files in six months (Image Credit: Thorn)

From the DNA Foundation to Thorn

How its technology helps investigators

Expanding research and child safety efforts

Technology has made it easier for children to connect with the world, but it has also created new ways for predators to exploit them. Tackling this problem requires more than removing harmful content after it appears online. It also involves identifying victims, helping investigators trace abuse and giving technology companies tools to detect exploitation. This challenge prompted actor Ashton Kutcher and Demi Moore to establish the DNA Foundation in 2009, which later became Thorn: Digital Defenders of Children, a technology-driven nonprofit focused on protecting children from sexual exploitation online.According to Thorn's August 11, 2026, mid-year impact update and its retrospective, Thorn at Ten: A Decade of Progress, the organisation detected 1,399,479 suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) files between January and June 2026. Its victim identification tools were also being used by 1,046 law enforcement agencies during the same period. Separately, Thorn's 2025 impact figures reported that its victim identification technology was being used in 40 countries. These figures highlight how the organisation has expanded its work from an initial anti-trafficking initiative into a wider effort to use technology against online child sexual abuse.Kutcher and Moore established the DNA Foundation in 2009 after learning about the scale of child sex trafficking and exploitation. Their initial focus was on raising awareness and bringing together organisations that could help prevent trafficking and protect vulnerable children.In November 2012, the foundation adopted the name Thorn: Digital Defenders of Children and refined its mission to focus more closely on the role of technology in child sexual exploitation. The organisation recognised that digital platforms could be used by offenders to target children, distribute abusive material and extend exploitation across geographical boundaries.Thorn subsequently began working with technology companies, researchers, law enforcement agencies and other child protection organisations to develop tools that could help identify victims and detect abusive content. One of its early initiatives was the Thorn Technology Task Force, which brought technology companies together to explore solutions to online child exploitation.A major part of Thorn's work involves helping law enforcement identify children depicted in suspected abuse material. Its Spotlight tool was developed to assist investigators in finding victims of child sex trafficking and exploitation. By organising information and helping investigators examine evidence more efficiently, the technology can reduce the time spent identifying children who may still be experiencing abuse.The organisation also develops tools for technology companies to detect child sexual abuse material on their platforms. Its Safer product helps content-hosting services detect, review and report suspected abusive material. These tools are intended to prevent such content from spreading and reduce the repeated victimisation of children whose abuse has been documented and circulated online.Thorn's 2026 mid-year update reported that its technology processed more than 1.09 trillion files between January and June to detect suspected child sexual abuse material. During this period, it identified nearly 1.4 million suspected CSAM files and 470,521 suspected instances of child sexual exploitation. The organisation also reported that 86 companies were using its CSAM detection products. These figures represent suspected material and instances identified by its systems, rather than a confirmed count of individual victims or proven criminal cases.Thorn's work extends beyond detection technology. It also conducts research into how children experience the internet and how online exploitation methods are changing. Its 2025 Youth Perspectives Report examined young people's online experiences, including emerging patterns involving artificial intelligence and access to age-restricted platforms.In the first half of 2026, the organisation also published research on Sadistic Online Exploitation, examining how violent online networks exploit weaknesses in existing child protection systems. The findings are intended to help investigators, technology companies, policymakers and caregivers better understand emerging risks. Another development during this period was the integration of Thorn's Grooming Detection technology into Hive's moderation platform. The organisation also introduced Context Labels to its Safer product, giving safety professionals additional information to assess suspected abusive content and prioritise investigations.Thorn's international reach has grown alongside these initiatives. Its 2025 impact report recorded that victim identification tools were being used in 40 countries, while its mid-2026 update reported 1,046 law enforcement agencies using its child victim detection tools.The organisation's progress reflects a broader shift in child protection, where technology companies, investigators and researchers increasingly need to work together. Although detecting suspected abusive material is only one part of the response, Thorn's work aims to help identify victims sooner, limit the circulation of harmful content and strengthen safeguards for children navigating the digital world.
Article Summary: Ashton Kutcher and Demi Moore established the DNA Foundation in 2009. In 2012, the foundation adopted the name Thorn: Digital Defenders of Children. Thorn works with technology companies, researchers, law enforcement agencies and other child protection organisations to develop tools that could help identify victims and detect abusive content. Its technology processed more than 1.09 trillion files between January and June to detect suspected child sexual abuse material.

Article Title: In 1990, a cockpit window blew out at 17,300 feet and sucked British Airways captain Tim Lancaster halfway out of his plane; crew members held his legs for about 20 minutes until the jet landed and he
Article Text:
AI's reconstruction of the 1990 incident in which British Airways captain was pulled halfway out of the cockpit

Crew responded quickly

Pilot suffered fractures and frostbite

A British Airways captain was nearly pulled out of his aircraft after a cockpit window shattered at 24,000 feet during a flight from England to Spain in June 1990. As the aircraft lost pressure, the force pulled the pilot's upper body through the broken window. Two crew members held on to him while the co-pilot took control and prepared for an emergency landing.According to Associated Press' then report, the incident took place on June 10, 1990, aboard British Airways flight 5390. The BAC-111 aircraft had taken off from Birmingham and was heading to Malaga, Spain, with 81 passengers and six crew members on board. Captain Tim Lancaster, 41, was flying the aircraft with co-pilot Alistair Atchison, 39.About 20 minutes after take-off, a cockpit window shattered. The sudden loss of pressure affected the flight deck and pulled Lancaster out of his seat. His head and shoulders were outside the aircraft, leaving the crew with little time to react.A steward in the forward galley heard a loud bang and saw what had happened. He rushed towards the cockpit and managed to grab Lancaster's legs. Another steward, Simon Rogers, joined him and helped restrain the captain.Their efforts prevented Lancaster from being pulled completely out of the aircraft.Meanwhile, Atchison took control of the aircraft and made an emergency call. He turned the plane around and prepared to land at Southampton Airport. The aircraft landed safely at around 9 am, ending an emergency that had put the captain's life at risk.A British Airways spokesman described the crew's response to the incident in comments reported by United Press International."One of the cabin crew went straight to the flight deck, where he managed to grab ahold of the captain, whose head and shoulders I believe were out the window," the spokesman said.He also explained how another steward helped hold Lancaster while the co-pilot concentrated on landing the aircraft. "A second steward, Simon Rogers, strapped himself into the captain's seat and restrained the captain while the first officer undertook the landing," he said.The co-pilot, Atchison, radioed a Mayday message to Eastleigh Airport in Southampton. He then brought the aircraft down safely. Southampton was about 76 miles south-west of London, according to the UPI report.The emergency landing allowed the passengers and crew to leave the aircraft safely. However, the incident had left several people shaken.Lancaster was taken to Southampton Hospital for treatment. He was listed in comfortable condition, according to the British Airways spokesman quoted by UPI.His injuries included fractures to his elbow, wrist and thumb. He also suffered frostbite to one hand and shock.The sudden loss of pressure in the cockpit had not affected the passenger cabin in the same way. However, six passengers and crew members were treated for shock and later released from hospital, UPI reported.British Airways arranged another aircraft for the passengers who wanted to continue their journey. Seventy-seven passengers travelled onwards to Malaga.The incident raised questions about what had caused the cockpit window to break during the flight. British Airways officials said they did not immediately know why the windscreen had shattered. Civil aviation investigators began examining the aircraft to establish the cause.
Article Summary: A cockpit window shattered at 24,000 feet during a flight from England to Spain in June 1990. The sudden loss of pressure affected the flight deck and pulled the pilot out of his seat. Two crew members held on to him while the co-pilot took control and prepared for an emergency landing.

Article Title: 2 killed as vehicle swept away by floodwaters in France's Corsica
Article Text:
Heavy rainfall on the French island of Corsica has recently led to flooding and tragic fatalities. (Pic Credit: X Handle)

Two people died after their vehicle was swept away by floodwaters triggered by heavy rainfall on the French island of Corsica, interior minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday.According to news agency Reuters, a 40-year-old woman was rescued following the incident, Nunez said. One of the firefighters involved in the rescue operation was also taken to hospital and is being treated for hypothermia.The incident comes as heavy rain and flooding continue to affect Corsica and parts of southern France. French weather agency meteo-France has issued warnings over the adverse weather conditions, cautioning residents about the risk of flooding.Authorities have recorded rainfall of up to 350 mm (13.8 inches) in some areas since the storm began on Wednesday afternoon.The heavy downpours have triggered flooding concerns across the region, prompting warnings from weather officials and emergency services.
Article Summary: Two people died after their vehicle was swept away by floodwaters triggered by heavy rainfall on the French island of Corsica. A 40-year-old woman was rescued following the incident. One of the firefighters involved in the rescue operation was also taken to hospital and is being treated for hypothermia.

Article Title: A Georgia homeowner returned from a two-week trip to find an attic leak, but his insurer paid $13,844 against a repair estimate exceeding $112,000; on November 4, an appeals court upheld the rejection
Article Text:
A Georgia appeals court rejected a homeowner's $112,000 repair claim over an attic leak. (AI image)

Why the homeowner's lawsuit failed

Appeals court upholds exclusion of expert evidence

Court finds no link between repairs and leak

A Georgia homeowner who returned from a two-week trip to find an attic leak has lost his lawsuit against his insurer. Torry Hull demanded more than $112,000 for repairs after Safeco Insurance Company of Indiana paid him about $13,844. On November 4, the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit upheld a lower court's ruling in favour of the insurer.According to the judgment , Hull discovered a leak from a condenser line in his attic and filed an insurance claim. Safeco sent an adjuster to inspect the property, who assessed the damage at $17,187.02. After deductions, the company paid Hull $13,843.85.Unhappy with the payment, Hull sought an independent estimate from Leading Public Adjuster Inc. It valued the repairs at $112,401.23 on a replacement-cost basis and $104,187.45 on an actual-cost basis.Hull demanded $112,401.23 from Safeco and threatened legal action if it refused. The insurer stood by its original payment. Hull then sued, alleging breach of contract and bad faith.Safeco argued that Hull had not provided admissible evidence linking the additional repairs to the attic leak. It said he could not establish that the disputed expenses were covered by his policy.Hull relied on the estimate and his testimony. He also sought to introduce evidence from Carlos Martorell, a public adjuster who helped prepare the estimate. However, he disclosed Martorell as an expert only after discovery had ended.Hull blamed the delay on a "clerical placement error". He argued that Safeco already knew about the estimate and had communicated with Martorell's employer.Safeco objected, saying it had lost the opportunity to question Martorell during discovery. The district court excluded his affidavit, ruling that the late disclosure was neither justified nor harmless.The court also found that the estimate did not connect the additional repairs to the leak. It lacked a "causation analysis, methodology, or other basis" to help a jury determine whether the expenses were covered.Hull's testimony was also insufficient. He lacked personal knowledge of the cause, scope and necessity of the repairs. The district court consequently ruled in Safeco's favour on both claims.Hull challenged the decision before the Eleventh Circuit. He argued that the district court should have accepted Martorell's affidavit and that the estimate and his deposition testimony established a genuine dispute over the damage.The appeals court examined Rule 37 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. It allows courts to exclude an expert's evidence if a party fails to disclose the witness during discovery, unless the failure was substantially justified or harmless.The court considered three factors: the importance of the testimony, the reason for the late disclosure and the prejudice caused to the opposing party.Only the first factor favoured Hull. Martorell's testimony was important because it could have helped establish that the additional repairs resulted from the leak.However, Hull failed to explain the late disclosure beyond calling it a "clerical placement error". The court said he was responsible for meeting his discovery obligations.The late disclosure also seriously affected Safeco. Since discovery had closed, the insurer had no opportunity to question Martorell about the estimate and the methods used to prepare it.The appeals court rejected Hull's argument that Safeco already had the estimate and knew about Martorell's employer. It said the insurer was not required to track down and question an undisclosed witness in case Hull later relied on that person's evidence. The court found no error in excluding Martorell's affidavit.The Eleventh Circuit then examined whether Hull could prove his claims without the affidavit. It found that the estimate merely listed repairs and their costs without explaining how they resulted from the attic leak. As an example, the court pointed to a $3,000 charge for tree removal. The estimate did not explain how the work was connected to the leak.Hull's deposition testimony did not help either. He admitted he was "not the estimator" and had neither prepared the estimate nor been involved in the construction work. He said he "just relied on what other people estimate".The court said he could not establish that the additional repairs were necessary or caused by the covered leak by relying on other people's estimates. It therefore upheld the decision on the breach-of-contract claim.The appeals court also rejected Hull's bad-faith claim. Under Georgia law, he had to establish that the additional damage was covered by the policy, that he demanded payment before filing the lawsuit and that Safeco refused payment in bad faith. The court found insufficient evidence that the additional repairs resulted from a covered loss.It also said Safeco had a reasonable basis for rejecting the demand. Its adjuster had inspected the home and concluded that the additional repairs were unrelated to the leak. Hull offered no evidence that this assessment was unfounded or unreasonable. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the ruling in Safeco's favour on both claims.
Article Summary: Torry Hull discovered a leak from a condenser line in his attic and filed an insurance claim. Safeco sent an adjuster to inspect the property, who assessed the damage at $17,187.02. After deductions, the company paid Hull $13,843.85. Hull demanded $112,401.23 from Safeco and threatened legal action if it refused.

Article Title: Women who scored higher on cognitive tests were rated as more hostile by teammates and got less help from them, in studies of 432 US business students and 394 Chinese finance workers, a pattern that d
Article Text:
According to this new study, intelligent women get less help from their teammates (Canva)

Women in the Workplace Progress Report 2026

Journal of Applied Psychology

When intelligence becomes a disadvantage: What the study found

What happens when intelligence becomes a disadvantage? Image- Canva

Journal of Applied Psychology

Understanding the Intersection of Gender and Cognitive Ability on Interpersonal Outcomes: A Multistudy Investigation

Why capable women are perceived differently: The gender gap in workplace support

Society expects women to retain a certain pre-decided role (Image- Canva)

Global Gender Gap Report 2026

“One is not born, but rather becomes a woman.” The famous quote was written by Simone de Beauvoir, a French author, academician and feminist. The quote captures the struggle of women to fit into roles defined by society rather than being allowed to shape their own identities and ambitions. From the way they are expected to walk to how they are expected to look and behave, everything is predetermined by society, and women even today continue to navigate through the expectations that men do not always face in the same way.If you are one of those who think these were the talks of older times, then you might want to reconsider. According to the, 49% of professional women cited company culture as the single greatest barrier to their career progression, surpassing pay disparity and direct promotion structural hurdles. Someone once said that the world is not made for women; they just learnt to walk through it. Sometimes, these barriers are not just about being directly denied opportunities but also about how women are perceived when they demonstrate their abilities.A recent study published in thereveals an unsettling example of this, finding that women who scored higher on cognitive ability tests were perceived as more hostile by their teammates and received less help from them.Interestingly, the same pattern did not hold for men.Most of us think our intelligence will become our advantage; it will help us get a job or in our studies. But what happens when the same intelligence acts against you? What if being intelligent makes it harder to fit in, earn the trust of colleagues or receive the support we need to succeed?A study published in the, titled, examines this rather uncomfortable possibility. Researchers studied 432 business students in the US and 394 finance professionals in China to understand how cognitive ability and gender influence relationships between colleagues.The findings revealed an interesting pattern. Women who scored higher on cognitive ability tests were more likely to be perceived as hostile by their teammates. These perceptions were associated with greater victimisation and less help from colleagues, both in work-related tasks and personal matters. In the Chinese workplace sample, highly capable women were also perceived as less communal.Interestingly, the same pattern did not hold for men. Men with higher cognitive scores did not face the same negative perceptions and, in the Chinese sample, were actually seen as less hostile and received more help from their colleagues.The researchers suggest that this may reflect the different expectations society places on men and women. While confidence and competence are often accepted as signs of leadership in men, women displaying similar qualities may be judged differently. Their abilities do not necessarily change, but the way others interpret their behaviour can.According to the World Economic Forum's (WEF), women account for 41.8% of the workforce across the 62 economies covered by LinkedIn data. However, their representation drops sharply as they move up the corporate ladder. From making up 46% of entry-level employees, women's representation falls to just 23% in the C-suite. In other words, the higher the position, the fewer women we see occupying it.So, what happens along the way?The study offers one possible explanation. Society has predetermined what the roles and ambitions of a man and woman must be. This is known as social role theory. In it, people associate men with qualities like ambition, confidence and assertiveness, while women are traditionally expected to be warm, cooperative and accommodating. These expectations can influence how the same behaviour is interpreted depending on who displays it.For instance, a man who speaks confidently, challenges an idea or takes charge of a discussion may be seen as decisive and capable. A woman displaying the same qualities, however, may be perceived as difficult, hostile or less approachable. This is closely linked to what researchers call the 'implied communality deficit', where women who demonstrate high levels of competence are perceived as lacking the warmth and cooperation traditionally expected of them.The consequences can extend beyond how colleagues describe them. When teammates perceive women more negatively, they may be less willing to offer help, collaborate or include them in important work-related interactions. Over time, such workplace dynamics can make professional growth more difficult, even when women have the skills and abilities required to succeed.This does not mean that every capable woman faces the same treatment or that workplace inequality can be explained by one factor alone. However, the findings do raise an important question: if women are judged not only by the work they do but also by whether their behaviour fits society's expectations of them, how equal are the opportunities available to them in the first place?
Article Summary: Researchers studied 432 business students in the US and 394 finance professionals in China to understand how cognitive ability and gender influence relationships between colleagues. Women who scored higher on cognitive ability tests were more likely to be perceived as hostile by their teammates. These perceptions were associated with greater victimisation and less help from colleagues. In the Chinese workplace sample, highly capable women were also perceived as less communal. Men with higher cognitive scores did not face the same negative perceptions and, in the Chinese sample, were actually seen as less hostile.

Article Title: Earthquake of magnitude 5.0 jolts China's Xinjiang region
Article Text:
China's Xinjiang hit by 5.0-magnitude earthquake, says NCS

An earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck China's Xinjiang region at 10:26 pm IST on Thursday, the National Centre for Seismology (NCS) said.According to the NCS, the earthquake was recorded at 22:26 IST.The earthquake's epicentre was located close to the international border between India and China.There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.
Article Summary: An earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck China's Xinjiang region at 10:26 pm IST on Thursday. The earthquake's epicentre was located close to the international border between India and China. There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

Article Title: Midterm losses, no exits: Marco Rubio rules out quitting, Donald Trump backs Pete Hegseth
Article Text:
File photo - US President Donald Trump speaks during a media conference as Marco Rubio, right, and Pete Hegseth listen

Rubio backs JD Vance for 2028 presidential race

White House rejects reports of Rubio's possible exit

US secretary of state Marco Rubio has dismissed reports that he is considering leaving the Trump administration following the Republican Party's setbacks in the midterm elections, saying that completing President Donald Trump's second term has “always been my plan”.In an interview with The New York Times, Rubio rejected speculation that he might step down ahead of a possible 2028 presidential campaign and declined to discuss his political ambitions.“Working for President Trump until the end of his term has always been my plan,” Rubio said, adding that he did not know where reports about his possible departure had originated.“I love the work I’m doing,” he said. “And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. I go, ‘Which one?’”Rubio, who also serves as Trump's national security adviser, refused to entertain questions about whether he was considering a presidential run in 2028.“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” he told the newspaper in his White House office. “I just won’t do it.”Rubio has previously indicated that he would support Vice President JD Vance if he decided to run for president in 2028.“JD is a very good friend of mine,” Rubio told NBC News in May. “If JD runs for president, I think he’d be a phenomenal candidate. I’ve said publicly, and I’ll say it again, I’ll be the first person to sign up and support him.”However, Vance's post-election assessment on Wednesday included criticism of the administration's approach to the Iran war, its policy on Israel and its messaging on the economy.The vice-president blamed the war with Iran for the Republicans' election setbacks and said voters had turned against the administration's position on Israel and its handling of economic concerns. Trump has closely aligned himself with Israel and dismissed concerns over affordability as a “hoax”.Asked whether he agreed with Vance's assessment, Rubio initially deflected, saying he was not “really involved in domestic politics”.However, Rubio acknowledged the political implications of the Iran war when he appeared alongside Trump at a rally in Kansas on Sunday. Trump praised the secretary of state and joked that he might have to fire him because he had become “too popular”.Explaining his presence at the rally, Rubio said he was travelling with the president as the designated national security official. He also acknowledged Trump's remarks that the war had been a factor in the election results.“Higher prices at the gas pump, I acknowledge, is not like the kind of thing you campaign on and brag about,” Rubio said.However, he defended Trump's decision to take action despite its potential political costs, saying the president “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for doing what he considered necessary.“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.The White House and the State Department have also rejected reports that Rubio could leave his position following the Republican setbacks.White House spokesperson Beni Rae Harmony described the reports as a fabricated hoax circulated by anonymous sources, while assistant secretary of state for global public affairs Dylan Johnson called them baseless fake news.The speculation over a possible administration shake-up has also involved defence secretary Pete Hegseth , whose handling of the Iran war has drawn criticism following the election losses.The White House has denied reports that Hegseth and Rubio might leave their positions. Trump told ABC News that he had received calls about Hegseth but had “every intention” of keeping him. He later praised the defence secretary, saying he had “done a fantastic job”.However, Republican Representative Thomas Massie has said he intends to move ahead with an effort to impeach Hegseth, with a resolution expected as early as next week. Hegseth has rejected the effort, describing it as a politically motivated attempt to undermine him.Separately, The Washington Post reported that Trump could be considering replacing General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command.Both have played significant roles in providing guidance on the Iran war.
Article Summary: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has dismissed reports that he is considering leaving the Trump administration following the Republican Party's setbacks in the midterm elections. In an interview with The New York Times, Rubio rejected speculation that he might step down ahead of a possible 2028 presidential campaign. The White House and the State Department have also rejected reports that Rubio could leave his position.

Article Title: Namaste Uncle Sam: Nithya Raman poised to become LA Mayor, as America's top two cities get desi touch
Article Text:
Elected LA mayor Nithya Raman and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Nithya Raman's background

How Socialists are storming across American cities:

Indian origin winners from the US midterm elections

Nithya Raman stood before supporters at a downtown Los Angeles brewery in June, struggling to hold back tears. The early primary election returns had placed her third in the race for mayor, behind incumbent Karen Bass and reality tv personality Spencer Pratt, and it looked like the end of the road for her. She gave what was almost a concession speech. Her father Venkit Raman, an IITian, comforted campaign workers, telling them her full name Nithya Varsha means 'everlasting monsoon,' and her political life would be replenished soon.It came sooner than anyone expected because after all this is the la la land of Hollywood where plot twists are common. And appropriately too enough considering her husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, is a successful television writer and producer whose credits include 30 Rock and Modern Family. A batch of late ballots that came in took Raman past Pratt to second place, and because Bass did not get 50 per cent of the vote, there would be a run-off election in November. Even then, few gave the 45-year old political tyro, with only six years of experience on the City Council, any chance. Raman herself had once supported Bass, and the 73-year old party stalwart had the backing of the Democratic establishment, including endorsements from Kamala Harris, Nancy Pelosi and Governor Gavin Newsom.She had experience, name recognition, and the advantage of incumbency.What Bass could not quite escape was the perception that Los Angeles is broken and she did not have the toolkit to fix it. The devastating January 2025 Palisades wildfire, which killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes, became a defining political liability. Bass was abroad when the mishap occurred and her handling of the disaster and recovery became a persistent political liability. Raman’s campaign ignited. She offered herself as the candidate of change, promising better housing, improved public services and more accountable government. An urban planner by training, she could talk about the nuts and bolts of city administration rather than simply deliver ideological sermons. On Tuesday night, her persistence paid off, and although the race has not been officially called, she is ahead by 25,000 votes and looks likely to seal the deal. She invited supporters to join her in a dance on Wednesday, the tears in June now forgotten.Raman's victory is more than an extraordinary personal turnaround. It is another major breakthrough for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the left-wing movement that has been steadily challenging the Democratic Party establishment. And for India, it provides an especially striking political subplot: New York and Los Angeles, America's two largest cities, will now be led by mayors of Indian origin, with Zohran Mamdani already in office in New York.What's even more striking: Long before Mamdani and Raman began making their mark in American municipal politics, several prominent Indian nationalists and intellectuals had encountered the country's radical political traditions first hand. Lala Lajpat Rai spent five years in the U.S between 1914 and 1919, establishing the India Home Rule League and publishing the journal Young India in New York. The radical humanist M.N. Roy arrived in the U.S in 1916 as a global itinerant, encountered American radicals and began studying socialism, subsequently moving to Mexico City, where he founded the Communist Party of Mexico in 1919. He later played a foundational role in establishing the Communist Party of India in 1920. B.R. Ambedkar, meanwhile, studied at Columbia University in NYC, encountering some of America's leading liberal and progressive intellectuals, including philosopher John Dewey. And Jayaprakash Narayan spent seven years in America (1922-1929), studying at Berkeley, Iowa, and Wisconsin, where he encountered Marxism and returned to India a committed socialist.All this was at a time socialism was enjoying considerable electoral popularity. In 1912, Socialist Party presidential candidate Eugene Debs won nearly a million votes, then about 6% of the national total. Socialists also held hundreds of municipal offices, including mayoralties. In fact, in the early 1950s Donald Trump’s father Fred Trump clashed with the folk singer Woody Guthrie, an avowed socialist, over racial segregation and housing discrimination in Brooklyn, causing him to write a song -- a scalding takedown of a predatory landlord -- titled “Old Man Trump" who stirred up racial hatred "in the bloodsport of the human heart. "Indeed, even in the modern era, the current upsurge of socialists did not emerge overnight. One of its earliest conspicuous faces was another Indian activist: Kshama Sawant, born in Pune and raised in Mumbai, who won a seat on Seattle's City Council in 2013. A former economics professor and member of Socialist Alternative rather than the DSA, Sawant became a prominent voice for a $15 minimum wage, rent control and taxing the wealthy. Her victory demonstrated that a politician openly identifying with socialism could win in an American city.Bernie Sanders subsequently took the argument national with his presidential campaigns in 2016 and 2020 bringing democratic socialism into mainstream political conversation, particularly among younger Americans frustrated by inequality, expensive healthcare, housing costs and the influence of corporate money. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's (AOC’s) stunning 2018 primary victory over veteran Democrat Joe Crowley gave the movement another national face. The election of Mamdani as New York mayor in 2025 was an even bigger breakthrough. Mamdani defeated Democratic political heavyweight Andrew Cuomo by campaigning on affordable housing, free bus services, universal childcare and a city government that would work for ordinary people.The movement now has a growing presence in municipal government. Besides Mamdani in New York, democratic socialist or DSA-affiliated mayors include Katie Wilson in Seattle, Janeese Lewis George in Washington DC, Emma Mulvaney-Stanak in Burlington, Robert Cantelmo in Ithaca and Eduardo Martinez in Richmond, California. In the mid-terms, six DSA-endorsed candidates have won seats in the House of Representatives: Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York (both backed by Mamdani), Melat Kiros in Colorado, Angela Gonzales-Torres in California, Donavan McKinney in Michigan and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. DSA members Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib also won re-election.The organisation's own election tracker reported victories across an even wider range of state and local contests, including in Florida, Maryland, Washington, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Vermont. The significance is not simply the number of elected socialists, but their willingness, like in the case of Raman v Bass, to challenge Democratic incumbents and party leadership rather than wait patiently for establishment approval.While their electoral success is undeniable, the jury is still out on their ability to translate ambitious promises of affordable housing, safer streets, better transport and sustainable municipal finances into reality. Governing New York or Seattle or LA is considerably more complicated than winning an election with a catchy slogan. Already, MAGA bros are cranking up right wing fearmongering with Conservative commentators Benny Johnson invoking scenarios of urban 'Armageddon' a favorite Trump theme.For now though the socialists are having their moment in the sun. The MAGA crowd is predicting an apocalypse, the billionaires are checking their property portfolios, and the Democratic establishment is wondering whether it should start taking out membership in the DSA. Raman and Mamdani now have the rather unenviable task of proving that running a city is not quite the same as running against one. In the process, America's urban political landscape is getting a makeover — and this time, the revolution has an Indian accent.
Article Summary: Nithya Raman and Zohran Mamdani are the new mayors of Los Angeles and New York City respectively. Raman's victory is another major breakthrough for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the left-wing movement that has been challenging the Democratic Party establishment.

Article Title: A Scottish wildlife rescuer saved a starving badger cub trapped in a cattle trough, but officials denied his request to keep her; now he is fighting to retain the animal he says cannot survive in the
Article Text:
Rescued from a cattle trough in April, Harriet was nursed back to health by ecologist Graeme Wilson.

From a desperate rescue to an unusual bond

Why the ecologist wants to keep Harriet

Wildlife experts raise concerns

Harriet's future remains uncertain

Images Courtesy: istock and BBC

A chance encounter with a helpless animal has turned into a complicated battle over wildlife protection, rehabilitation and the limits of human intervention. When Scottish ecologist Graeme Wilson rescued a starving badger cub from a cattle trough, he expected to nurse her back to health. Instead, the experience left him convinced that returning her to the wild could put her life in danger. Now, he is fighting for permission to give Harriet a permanent home, despite opposition from wildlife authorities.According to the BBC, Harriet was discovered in April trapped inside a cattle trough, around 100 metres from her sett in the Scottish Borders. Wilson was called to help the young animal and took responsibility for her recovery, gradually nursing her back to health.However, her behaviour soon raised concerns about whether she could survive independently. Given her bottle feeding response and familiarity with humans, Wilson suspected Harriet was hand-reared before her rescue.As reported by The Telegraph, Wilson believes the cub has become accustomed to humans to such an extent that releasing her into the countryside could expose her to serious risks. He fears she might approach people while out walking, potentially placing herself in a dangerous situation.Wilson operates GW Ecology, an independent wildlife rescue and rehabilitation service from his home in Denholm. Alongside caring for injured animals, his work involves ecological surveys to identify protected species at proposed development sites. He also organises bat walks, workshops and educational activities to encourage greater awareness of wildlife conservation.The ecologist applied to NatureScot for an educational licence that would allow him to continue caring for Harriet while helping the public understand badgers and the challenges involved in rehabilitating protected wildlife.However, the application was rejected. NatureScot suggested that Harriet should either be returned to the wild or transferred to a zoo. Wilson believes neither option would adequately address her circumstances. While a release could expose her to injury or death, he fears a conventional zoo environment would leave her isolated and distressed.The disagreement has brought wider questions about the responsibilities involved in wildlife rehabilitation into focus. The BBC reported that the British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council has stressed the specialist nature of caring for wild animals.Paul Reynolds, who chairs the organisation, has highlighted the importance of suitable facilities, species-specific care, veterinary supervision and an understanding of an animal's natural behaviour. The council also distinguishes responsible rehabilitation from keeping wild animals permanently in captivity for educational or personal purposes.According to The Telegraph, the organisation maintains that an animal becoming accustomed to human contact should not automatically be considered grounds for permanent captivity.NatureScot has indicated that discussions with Wilson and other relevant organisations are continuing in an effort to find a practical resolution. The authority has emphasised that Harriet's welfare remains central to its decision-making process. Police Scotland has also been made aware of the situation.Meanwhile, the Scottish SPCA advises people who encounter sick or injured badgers to contact its rescue officers rather than attempting to handle the animals themselves. Young cubs found away from their setts may need help, and frightened or injured badgers may attack.Wilson still wants a safe future for Harriet. Whether that means an exception to the usual rules or another arrangement, the case highlights the difficult balance between individual animal welfare and the principles of wildlife conservation.
Article Summary: Harriet the badger cub was rescued from a cattle trough in April. Ecologist Graeme Wilson nursed her back to health but is now fighting for permission to give her a permanent home. The British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council has stressed the specialist nature of caring for wild animals.

Article Title: North Dakota gets its first life-size Mahatma Gandhi statue
Article Text: Mahatma Gandhi's first life-size statue in North Dakota was unveiled at Peace Park in downtown Bismarck, the state capital, on October 29, marking a new addition to India's cultural presence in the United States.The statue was installed with the assistance of the Consulate General of India in Seattle, with support from the Indian-American community and the North Dakota Trade Office. The ceremony was attended by North Dakota First Lady Kjersti Armstrong, Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring and India's Consul General in Seattle.Located at 400 East Front Avenue, Peace Park was developed following the September 11, 2001, attacks. It also houses a Peace Pole installed by the Gandhi Peace Network of North Dakota.With the Bismarck installation, the number of Gandhi monuments within the jurisdiction of the Indian Consulate in Seattle has risen to five. The other locations are Bellevue Public Library, Seattle's Space Needle, the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln and the University of Montana in Missoula.The Consulate said India-North Dakota ties have grown through engagements in agriculture, business, education and cultural activities, including International Day of Yoga celebrations and consular outreach in Fargo.

The number of Gandhi monuments within the jurisdiction of the Indian Consulate in Seattle has risen to five. The other locations are Bellevue Public Library, Seattle's Space Needle, the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln and the University of Montana in Missoula.

Article Title: A Florida couple disputed four reversed mortgage payments and stopped paying in 2017; an appeals court revived foreclosure proceedings despite the bank's accounting errors
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Four mortgage payments were reversed

Bank filed foreclosure proceedings

Appeals court found later missed payments established default

Foreclosure case sent back for further proceedings

A mortgage dispute can become complicated when a lender's own accounting records leave borrowers questioning how much they owe. A Florida couple faced this situation after their bank reversed four mortgage payments made in 2015 without explaining why. Although they continued making monthly payments for nearly two more years, the lender eventually refused to accept further payments, and the couple stopped paying. The dispute eventually reached an appeals court after a trial judge ruled that the bank had failed to prove a mortgage default.In an opinion dated November 4, 2026, Florida's Second District Court of Appeal reversed that decision in The Bank of New York Mellon v. Fernandez, case number 2D2025-1819. The ruling , available on Justia, revived the bank's foreclosure case against Michael and Dianna Fernandez. However, the court also directed the lower court to exclude the four disputed payments and certain related interest and fees when calculating the outstanding debt.Michael and Dianna Fernandez signed a $160,000 mortgage note in 2007, secured by their home. In 2012, they filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy and subsequently entered into a mortgage modification agreement with the loan servicer. At the time, Bank of America was servicing the loan on behalf of The Bank of New York Mellon.On August 21, 2015, the bank reversed four mortgage payments the couple had made earlier that year, between January and April.However, the payment records did not explain why the transactions had been reversed. At the trial, the bank's representative could not provide a definite reason and could only speculate about the circumstances that might normally cause such reversals. Dianna testified that she had made all four payments and that the money had never been returned to her. The reversals placed the loan four payments behind according to the bank's records. Despite this, the couple continued making monthly payments from August 2015 through April 2017, and the bank accepted them.The situation changed in May 2017, when Bank of America returned their payment because it was insufficient to cover the amount the bank claimed was outstanding, including the four reversed payments. Dianna also visited a bank branch approximately twice that month to make a payment, but the bank refused to accept it.In 2017, the bank initially filed a foreclosure lawsuit but voluntarily dismissed it before trial. In January 2021, it filed another foreclosure action, claiming the couple had defaulted on payments beginning January 1, 2017, and all subsequent installments. The Fernandezes disputed the allegation, arguing that they had made their payments until the bank stopped accepting them. They also maintained that the lender's own actions had created the alleged default.During the bench trial, Dianna acknowledged that the couple's last accepted payment was made in April 2017. She also admitted that they had not made further payments and did not have sufficient funds to bring the mortgage current when the new foreclosure action was filed. The trial judge ruled in the couple's favour, finding that the bank had failed to establish a default. The judge relied on the unexplained reversal of the four earlier payments, Dianna's credible testimony and the bank's decision to return the May 2017 payment and refuse subsequent attempts to pay. The bank appealed the judgment.The appeals court agreed that the bank had failed to explain the four reversed payments. However, it found that this accounting problem did not eliminate the couple's separate obligation to continue making their monthly mortgage payments. The majority pointed out that the undisputed evidence showed the couple had not made payments from June 2017 onwards. Each missed monthly installment constituted a separate default under Florida law.The court explained that a disagreement over how a lender accounts for earlier payments does not automatically excuse borrowers from continuing to meet their mortgage obligations. Even if the four earlier payments were improperly reversed, the couple still had to make subsequent payments. The court also rejected the couple's argument that the bank's refusal to accept payments amounted to unclean hands. It found insufficient evidence of fraud, dishonest conduct or wrongdoing that would legally prevent the bank from pursuing foreclosure.The majority further noted that the couple had not formally tendered their unpaid installments by depositing the money with the court or otherwise demonstrating that they had the amount due when the lawsuit began.The Florida Court of Appeal reversed the trial court's judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings. It instructed the lower court to remove the principal amount of the four reversed payments, interest accrued before June 2017 and any fees charged before July 2017. The court also allowed the lower court to consider reducing attorney fees for work spent disputing the four reversed payments. Judge Silberman dissented, arguing that the trial court's findings were supported by the evidence. He maintained that the bank's unexplained accounting reversals, returned payment and refusal to accept subsequent installments had effectively created and prolonged the default.The ruling does not mean the couple has immediately lost their home. It restores the foreclosure proceedings while requiring the disputed accounting entries and related charges to be excluded from the debt calculation. The appeals court also noted that the couple could still explore options to retain their property, including redeeming the mortgage debt under Florida law or pursuing available federal bankruptcy protections.

Article Title: Rocky Balboa, Superman Cash, Fat Boy: Trio charged for using AI to steal $129 million in US
Article Text:
The 3 were indicted for allegedly using AI to impersonate CEOs, lawyers

Three people with nicknames including “Rocky Balboa”, “Superman Cash” and “Fat Boy” have been indicted in the US for allegedly using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that targeted thousands of companies worldwide and stole around $129 million.Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, face charges of wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering, according to an indictment filed in a US District Court in New York. The alleged scheme ran for more than 18 months and targeted businesses across several countries, reported AP.According to court documents, the accused primarily targeted corporate accounting departments. They allegedly sent emails posing as company CEOs, asking employees to facilitate confidential financial transactions. The requests were followed by phone or video calls in which the defendants used AI to mimic the executives' voices and, in some cases, their appearances.The group would then direct employees to contact an attorney at a major law firm, whom they were also prepared to impersonate. Soall allegedly posed as UK-based lawyers and had a “handwritten script titled ‘Lawyer Call’” to make himself appear genuine while speaking to victims, according to the US attorney's office.Employees were subsequently instructed to transfer large sums to bank accounts across the world. The money was then converted into cryptocurrency to conceal its origins before being distributed among the accused and others involved, the indictment said.The alleged victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a Rhode Island bank, a UK-based financial technology company, a Massachusetts mutual fund company and a Florida pet food company.The three defendants, who are from Spain, the UK, Israel and the United Arab Emirates, were arrested between June and September. Hazan was previously convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in a New York court in 2008.FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C Barnacle Jr said the case highlighted how emerging technology could be exploited for large-scale fraud.“As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities,” he said.Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It was unclear whether Hazan had legal representation.If convicted, the defendants face a maximum sentence of 20 years on each wire fraud and money laundering charge, while aggravated identity theft carries a mandatory additional two-year sentence, according to the US attorney's office.
Article Summary: Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, face charges of wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering. The alleged scheme ran for more than 18 months and targeted businesses across several countries. They allegedly sent emails posing as company CEOs, asking employees to facilitate confidential financial transactions.

Article Title: In 2016, a Texas nursing aide was injured when a patient weighing over 300 pounds fell on her; 10 years later, an appeals court upheld liability on a $7.11 million verdict but offered a $264,448 cut o
Article Text:
CNAs were to receive two days of general training and three days of nurse-supervised floor training. (AI image)

Nursing aide received only one day of floor training

Patient fell during wheelchair transfer

Court finds facility failed to provide adequate training

Court cuts future medical expenses

Court upholds physical impairment awards

The Texas Court of Appeals has upheld a nursing facility's liability in a lawsuit filed by a nursing aide who was injured while helping a patient weighing more than 300 pounds move from a bed to a wheelchair. However, it has proposed reducing the $500,000 awarded for her future medical expenses by $264,448.51.The ruling , delivered by the Fourteenth Court of Appeals on November 5, comes nearly 10 years after the May 2016 incident. The court upheld the jury's finding that Red Bluff LLC was negligent and that its actions caused the aide's injuries.The jury awarded Nicole Tarpley $7.11 million for medical expenses, physical pain, mental anguish and physical impairment. The appeals court upheld most of the award but said the evidence supported only $235,551.49 in future medical expenses.Tarpley has 20 days to accept the proposed reduction. Otherwise, the case will return to the trial court for a new trial on liability and damages.Red Bluff operates a nursing and rehabilitation facility in Pasadena, Texas. It hired Tarpley as a certified nursing assistant (CNA) in April 2016. She had five years of experience but had worked at the facility for only three weeks when the accident happened.The facility's assistant director of nursing, Lisa Kemp, said new CNAs were supposed to receive two days of general training and three days of floor training while shadowing a nurse. Tarpley received only one day of floor training before being told she was "ready".During her training, Tarpley was instructed that a resident identified as Tom, who weighed more than 300 pounds, needed only one person to help him move from his bed to a wheelchair.On May 5, 2016, Tom asked Tarpley to help him move from his room to the library. She placed a walker beside his bed and positioned a wheelchair next to it, locking its brakes.Tom stood up holding the walker while Tarpley steadied him with one hand and held the wheelchair with the other. Although she checked the brakes again, the wheelchair moved when they unexpectedly disengaged.As Tom began falling, Tarpley tried to support him with her leg. Her knee hyperextended, and her body twisted as they both fell. She heard a "clack" in her knee but continued working after seeking help.Kemp later testified that Tom required at least two employees for transfers because of his weight and the risk of falling. She said she would not have attempted to move him without assistance.Red Bluff's corporate representative, Adeyemi Alabi-Isama, also said a CNA should not have attempted the transfer alone without additional training from a physical therapist.Tarpley's expert, registered nurse and CNA instructor Donna Raley, testified that the aide had not been properly trained. She said Red Bluff had failed to provide adequate instructions on transferring residents, particularly Tom.Red Bluff argued that Tarpley had five years of CNA experience and should have understood the risks of moving a patient weighing more than 300 pounds without assistance.The appeals court disagreed, noting that transferring patients, particularly heavy ones, involved procedures requiring specific knowledge and training.It also pointed out that Red Bluff had instructed Tarpley on how to move Tom. Having undertaken to provide the training, the facility had a duty to ensure its instructions were adequate.The court found sufficient evidence that Red Bluff had failed to exercise ordinary care in training Tarpley. It upheld the jury's negligence finding and said there was no need to examine the separate premises-liability finding.The appeals court separately examined the $500,000 awarded for future medical expenses. Tarpley suffered injuries to her knee, neck and lower back. She developed herniated discs and eventually underwent discectomy and fusion surgery at two levels in her neck.Her surgeon, Dr Henry Small, testified that she would need another operation on an adjacent level of her neck. He estimated its cost at $235,551.49, the same as her first surgery.For her lower back, the doctor recommended a spinal cord stimulator. However, Tarpley presented no evidence of its likely cost.The court therefore found evidence supporting future medical expenses of $235,551.49, but not the full $500,000 awarded by the jury. It proposed reducing the award by $264,448.51.Red Bluff also challenged the jury's awards of $750,000 for past physical impairment and $2 million for future physical impairment. The appeals court rejected the challenge.Tarpley told the court that her knee continued to "click and pop" and that she could no longer walk as she did before the accident. She also described persistent back pain, neck pain and migraines.She said she could no longer lift or play with her children or go camping with them. Although surgery improved her neck condition, her range of motion remained about 60% of what it was before the accident.Her injuries also affected activities she shared with her husband, including antiquing and restoring furniture. She could no longer stand for long periods or lift furniture.Her husband was later diagnosed with terminal stage 4 lung cancer, which spread to his bones and left him wheelchair-bound. Tarpley said she could not lift him into his wheelchair or help him bathe.The court said her testimony showed that the injuries had affected her daily activities and hobbies beyond physical pain and mental anguish. It upheld both physical impairment awards.
Article Summary: Court finds facility failed to provide adequate training. Court cuts future medical expenses by $264,448.51. Nicole Tarpley suffered injuries to her knee, neck and lower back. She developed herniated discs and eventually underwent discectomy and fusion surgery in her neck.

Article Title: After their father died in Saudi Arabia in 2009, a New York man alleged his mother and sister broke promises involving homes in Pennsylvania and Long Island; a November 5 court ruling has dismissed hi
Article Text:
Ahmed v Choudhry

Dispute over two properties and father's estate

Court says man waited too long to pursue claims

Fraud and misappropriation claims also rejected

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think Ahmed should have waited longer to file his lawsuit? Yes, he should have waited longer No, he acted within a reasonable time 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A family dispute over inherited assets, property promises and two homes in the United States has ended with a New York court dismissing a man's lawsuit against his mother and sister. According to a judgment published on the legal database Justia on November 5, 2026, the New York Appellate Division, First Department, in(2026 NY Slip Op 06518), upheld the dismissal of Saad Ahmed's complaint. Ahmed had alleged that his mother and sister failed to honour promises involving a property in Pennsylvania and another on Long Island after his father, Mahmood Choudhry, died in Saudi Arabia in December 2009. The appellate court unanimously upheld the earlier decision, ruling that several claims were filed beyond the applicable legal time limits.The case, Ahmed v Choudhry, centred on allegations that Ahmed's mother, Shahla Choudhry, and sister, Nazia Ahmed, had repeatedly assured him that ownership of the Pennsylvania property would eventually be transferred to him. He claimed that he relied on these assurances for years but never received the promised title.He also alleged that his family misrepresented their financial circumstances, leading him to purchase a Long Island property because his mother supposedly had no money and needed a place to live.The appellate court's ruling did not establish whether the alleged family promises were made or whether the disputed representations were true. Instead, it upheld the dismissal primarily because Ahmed had failed to bring several claims within the prescribed limitation periods and had not demonstrated sufficient legal grounds to revive them.According to the court judgment, the dispute also involved the distribution of Mahmood Choudhry's assets following his death. Ahmed alleged that his father's estate had been distributed in 2009 or 2010, but claimed that certain assets had been concealed or misappropriated by his family members.One of the central disagreements concerned the Pennsylvania property. Ahmed claimed that his mother and sister repeatedly assured him that its title would be transferred to him. However, despite the alleged promise, the transfer had not taken place by December 2016. He argued that he continued relying on their assurances and expected the agreement to be honoured.The second dispute concerned a property on Long Island. Ahmed alleged that his family persuaded him to purchase it in 2016 by falsely claiming that they had no money and that his mother needed accommodation. He claimed that the arrangement involved promises of rental payments, but Shahla allegedly stopped making the payments in November 2020.Ahmed further alleged that he discovered concealed family assets in January 2019. He also stated that his mother and sister had repudiated their alleged agreement in 2021, leaving him without the property arrangements he claimed had been promised.The legal battle eventually reached the New York Supreme Court, where the defendants sought dismissal of the complaint. On May 21, 2025, the court granted their request and dismissed the lawsuit in its entirety. Ahmed challenged that decision before the Appellate Division, First Department.In its November 5 ruling, the appellate court unanimously affirmed the earlier dismissal. The judges noted that several claims, including those involving breach of contract, unjust enrichment and quantum meruit, were subject to a six-year statute of limitations. Ahmed did not dispute that the six-year period applied but argued that equitable estoppel and fraudulent concealment should prevent his family from relying on those deadlines.However, the court found that he had failed to demonstrate the necessary diligence in pursuing his claims. It pointed to his own account of events, including the failure to transfer the Pennsylvania property in 2016, his discovery of allegedly concealed assets in January 2019 and the alleged repudiation of the agreement in 2021.The judgment also referred to text messages exchanged in October 2022, which showed that Ahmed was aware of potential legal claims and was consulting a lawyer. Despite this, he waited another year and four months before filing the lawsuit in February 2024.The judges said his continued reliance on the alleged promises for more than eight years was not reasonable, particularly given the repeated failure to transfer the Pennsylvania property's title. They also rejected his argument that the defendants' alleged concealment could revive claims that had already become time-barred.The court separately examined Ahmed's allegations of fraud, conversion, misappropriation of funds and civil embezzlement. It noted that he had not directly addressed the dismissal of several of these claims in his original opposition to the defendants' motion.Even when considered separately, the claims faced legal obstacles. The court explained that conversion claims were subject to a three-year limitation period and that the alleged misappropriation of his father's estate assets dated back to their distribution in 2009 or 2010.It also clarified that civil embezzlement was not recognised as an independent legal cause of action under New York law. The fraud claims relating to the Long Island property were also dismissed as untimely. Ahmed had alleged that he discovered the supposedly false representations in January 2019 but did not commence proceedings until February 2024.His requests for attorneys' fees and punitive damages were rejected as well. The court said attorneys' fees could not be pursued as a separate cause of action in this case, while the allegations did not meet the requirements for punitive damages.Ahmed also sought permission to amend his complaint, but the appellate judges concluded that doing so would be futile because the proposed changes could not correct the underlying legal defects.The November 5 decision leaves the May 2025 dismissal intact, ending this appeal over the disputed Pennsylvania and Long Island properties. The ruling underscores how limitation periods and delays in pursuing legal remedies can affect even complicated family disputes involving inheritance, property ownership and alleged financial promises.
Article Summary: Saad Ahmed alleged that his mother and sister failed to honour promises involving a property in Pennsylvania and another on Long Island. The dispute also involved the distribution of Mahmood Choudhry's assets following his death. The New York Appellate Division, First Department, in(2026 NY Slip Op 06518), upheld the dismissal of Ahmed's complaint.

Article Title: In 2009, Bob Dylan released his first-ever Christmas album that surprised his fans; the music legend donated all its royalties to charities feeding millions of people and pledged future earnings from
Article Text:
Bob Dylan's first Christmas album came with an unusual charitable promise

Three charities were selected to receive royalties from the album

Feeding America received the US royalties

Crisis was chosen to support homeless people in Britain

World Food Programme was assigned royalties for school meals

Bob Dylan explained why he chose the three charities

How the international royalties were channelled to charities

What made Christmas in the Heart different from other Christmas albums?

The album reached the top of Billboard's holiday chart

Dylan's promise extended beyond the 2009 holiday season

When legendary singer-songwriter Bob Dylan announced his first-ever Christmas album in 2009, the release came with an unusual promise. Rather than keeping the royalties generated by the record, the musician decided to donate them to organisations working to fight hunger and homelessness across the world. Titled Christmas in the Heart, the album featured 15 traditional Christmas songs and was released on October 13, 2009. Dylan pledged all his US artist royalties to Feeding America, while international earnings were directed towards the World Food Programme and British homelessness charity Crisis. The arrangement also covered future royalties in perpetuity, turning the holiday record into a continuing source of support for charitable causes.The announcement was made on August 26, 2009, when Columbia Records confirmed that Christmas in the Heart would be released in October.For Dylan, whose career had largely been associated with folk, rock and socially conscious songwriting, a Christmas album was an unexpected musical departure. However, the charitable commitment attached to it made the project particularly distinctive.Dylan announced that he would donate all his US artist royalties from the album to Feeding America, a nationwide network of food banks and hunger-relief organisations.The commitment extended beyond the initial release, with future US royalties also pledged to the organisation in perpetuity.International royalties were assigned to two other organisations: the World Food Programme, which works to address hunger in developing countries, and Crisis, a British charity supporting people experiencing homelessness.In his announcement, Dylan highlighted the scale of food insecurity in the US, noting that more than 35 million people, including 12 million children, were affected. He expressed hope that the project would help improve food security for people struggling to access regular meals.The initiative was structured around three organisations working in different parts of the world, allowing the proceeds to support people facing hunger and homelessness across several communities.Feeding America was selected to receive all of Dylan's artist royalties generated in the United States. The organisation operates a nationwide network of food banks and community-based agencies that distribute food to people facing hunger.At the time, Vicki Escarra, then president and chief executive of Feeding America, said the organisation had initially approached Dylan without expecting him to make such an extensive commitment.The initial arrangement was expected to generate more than four million meals for over 1.4 million people in the US during the holiday season.The UK-based charity Crisis was designated to receive international royalties for its work supporting people experiencing homelessness.The initial commitment was expected to provide 15,000 meals to homeless people in Britain between December 23 and January 1.Crisis works with people facing homelessness through accommodation, practical assistance, education, employment support and other services designed to help them move towards more stable living conditions.The United Nations World Food Programme was selected to receive another share of the international royalties.The initial initiative was expected to support 500,000 meals for schoolchildren in developing countries. School meal programmes are an important part of the agency's work, helping children access nutritious food while encouraging school attendance.The three organisations were therefore expected to benefit from the same album through different hunger-relief and humanitarian programmes.In an October 2009 interview with journalist Bill Flanagan, published by Street Roots on December 10, Dylan was asked why he had selected the three organisations for the project.His response offered a glimpse into the thinking behind the decision. He said he chose them because they delivered food directly to people who needed it, rather than relying on complicated administrative structures."Because they get food straight to the people. No military organization, no bureaucracy, no governments to deal with," Dylan explained.During the conversation, he also discussed his relationship with Christmas music. Although he grew up in a Jewish family in Hibbing, Minnesota, he recalled being surrounded by Christmas traditions, including carollers, church bells, snow and Nativity plays.He described the songs as familiar parts of his life and said he approached the recordings sincerely rather than as a humorous experiment.The international side of the initiative involved a separate financial arrangement to ensure that royalties generated outside the US could reach the designated organisations.In December 2009, Columbia/Epic worked with CAF America, an organisation specialising in international charitable giving, to establish a donor-advised fund for distributing the overseas royalties.A December 15, 2009 report by InvestmentNews revealed that the international royalty fund had already generated $125,000 for charitable distribution.The arrangement was also notable because CAF America described it as apparently the first time a donor-advised fund had been used to channel royalties from a major music recording towards charitable foundations.The money was intended to support the commitments made to Crisis and the World Food Programme, including meals for homeless people in Britain and schoolchildren in developing countries.Released on October 13, 2009, through Columbia Records, Christmas in the Heart marked Dylan's first full-length Christmas album. It contained 15 traditional Christmas songs, hymns and holiday standards.The tracklist included familiar festive recordings such as Here Comes Santa Claus, Winter Wonderland, Little Drummer Boy, Silver Bells, Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas and O Little Town of Bethlehem.The album also featured Must Be Santa, a traditional Christmas song that Dylan performed with a lively arrangement.The recording brought together musicians associated with his touring band, along with guitarist David Hidalgo of Los Lobos and guitarist Phil Upchurch. Dylan used the production pseudonym Jack Frost, which he had also employed on other recording projects.The arrangements retained a traditional holiday sound, with brass, backing vocals and country-influenced instrumentation complementing Dylan's distinctive voice.Despite being an unusual release in Dylan's extensive musical career, Christmas in the Heart attracted considerable commercial attention.The album debuted at No. 23 on the Billboard 200, selling approximately 20,000 copies during its first week in the US, according to contemporary music industry reporting.It also reached No. 1 on Billboard's Top Holiday Albums chart and the US Folk Albums chart.Its commercial performance was important to the charitable arrangement because sales generated royalties that could be directed towards the participating organisations.The most distinctive part of the arrangement was its long-term nature. Dylan did not limit his commitment to the album's initial sales or the Christmas season in which it was released.His pledge covered future US artist royalties in perpetuity, while the international royalty arrangement was also designed to continue supporting the selected charities.This meant that subsequent earnings generated by the album could continue contributing to hunger-relief and homelessness programmes long after its original release.The initiative brought together Dylan's music, the work of three established humanitarian organisations and a continuing royalty commitment that was intended to support people facing food insecurity.
Article Summary: Bob Dylan's first-ever Christmas album, Christmas in the Heart, was released in October 2009. The musician pledged to donate all US artist royalties to Feeding America. International earnings were directed towards the World Food Programme and Crisis. Dylan said he chose the charities because they delivered food directly to people.

Article Title: ‘Diversity is our strength’: Five US states, 21 cities host first-ever Diwali celebrations at official venues
Article Text:
Diwali celebrations hosted for first time at US state capitols, governors' mansions across Pacific Northwest

US governors recognise Indian American community's contributions

21 cities host Diwali ceremonies, more events scheduled

Washington recognises Diwali as state observance

Governors of five US states and mayors of 21 cities across the Pacific Northwest have hosted Diwali celebrations for the first time at state capitols, governors' mansions and city halls, with the Indian American community's contributions to their regions receiving recognition from local leaders.The celebrations, described by the Consulate General of India in Seattle as among the largest-ever Diwali events hosted across the US Pacific Northwest, began in mid-October and will continue until November 10, 2026.The governor of Oregon is scheduled to host the final ceremony at the State Capitol in Salem on that date.Governors of Idaho, Nebraska, Montana, North Dakota and Washington hosted the first-ever state-level celebrations at their respective governors' mansions and state capitol rotundas.The events were attended by US senators, members of Congress, local mayors and Indian American community leaders, the Consulate said in a press release dated November 5.During the celebrations, state leaders highlighted the contributions of Indian Americans to their respective states' economies, professions, public service and cultural diversity.Idaho governor Brad Little, speaking at the State Capitol on October 16, said the Indian American community had strengthened the state's economy and local communities.“Here in Idaho, we’re proud to have a vibrant Indian community that contributes very much to our state through their businesses, professions, service and civic involvement. Indian Americans help strengthen Idaho’s economy and help our communities be better places to live, work and raise a family,” he said.At the Nebraska governor's Mansion in Lincoln on October 20, governor Jim Pillen described the Indian community as an important part of the state and urged families to preserve their traditions.“The Indian community is an incredibly vital piece of who we are as the people of Nebraska... It’s really important that you keep these traditions alive in your families. Never, ever, ever let the light go out!” Pillen said.North Dakota governor Kelly Armstrong, speaking at the governor's Residence in Bismarck on October 29, highlighted the importance of ties between the Indian American community and the state.“We should celebrate these relationships. We should celebrate these friendships. Diversity is our strength,” he said, adding that the relationship would continue at international, trade, state-to-state, diplomatic and human levels.Washington governor Bob Ferguson, addressing the celebration at the State Capitol Rotunda in Olympia on November 4, said the state was home to one of the largest shares of Indian Americans in the country.“And during the previous decade, we had the fastest-growing Indian American population in the entire country.
